title: Information-Gain Calibrated On-Policy Distillation for Deep Search Agents
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has recently emerged as a promising approach for transferring the capabilities of large agents to compact students. In deep search, where agents iteratively retrieve external evidence, a teacher's preference among plausible queries before retrieval may not predict which queries will return useful evidence. Standard OPD nevertheless supervises each student query from the preceding context alone, inducing a failure mode we term \textbf{\textit{evidence-blind supervision (EBS)}}. To understand this, we regroup the OPD objective by interaction turns and reveal two implicit priors: a \textit{budget prior} that allocates supervision by token volume, and a \textit{direction prior} that favors tokens preferred by the teacher, neither of which accounts for the evidence returned by the current query. Our empirical analysis shows that both priors contribute to EBS in practice: the first search turn accounts for 51.1\% of total absolute information gain but receives only 18.0\% of the supervision budget, while 43.7\% of search queries have teacher rewards that disagree in sign with post-retrieval information utility. To mitigate this, we propose \ours, which uses post-retrieval information gain (IG) to calibrate both priors: reallocating supervision toward information-critical turns while calibrating query preferences using the utility of retrieved evidence. Experiments on six multimodal search benchmarks show that \ours improves average accuracy by 3.4 and 1.7 percentage points for 2B and 4B students over standard OPD, enabling the 4B student to surpass its 8B teacher on MMSearch and BrowseComp-VL.

title: TransX Technical Report: Scaling Sequence Transduction for Recommendation
summary:
We present TransX, a sequence-transduction framework and co-designed infrastructure for scaling industrial recommendation with explicit control over model-compute allocation and execution amortization. TransX separates sequence encoding, behavior memory, and candidate-conditioned fusion into independently scalable components. Training amortizes causal trajectory computation across behavioral prefixes and fans out memory states to candidates; serving disaggregates bulk prefill, nearline refresh, and online prediction through compact behavior-memory KV.
  We observe anisotropic scaling returns: encoder scaling may saturate beyond moderate depth at fixed memory resolution and fusion capacity; increasing supervision shifts the allocation frontier toward candidate-conditioned fusion; and the memory resolution needed to preserve quality remains roughly stable as model capacity grows. We train TransX on click and conversion, post-train its shared behavioral interface for retrieval and preference ranking, and explore generative recommendation offline.
  In separate production A/B experiments, the core TransX model improves CTR by 6.02% and conversion by 4.45%, while post-trained retrieval and preference-ranking variants improve CTR by 2.96% and conversion by 1.33%, respectively, over corresponding production baselines. Under matched training conditions, the training infrastructure increases supervised-target throughput by 84%. In serving, disaggregation reduces TransX's total serving cost by nearly 80% versus colocated serving at matched traffic and SLO, enabling approximately 5X the per-request model FLOPs of the HSTU-style production baseline at the same total serving cost. At matched per-request model FLOPs, TransX delivers approximately 4X higher request throughput per H200. These results show that online serving cost need not grow proportionally with recommendation model capacity.

title: Learning Rewards in Strategic Games
summary: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.

title: The Komlós Problem in Matrix-Multiplication Time
summary: We give a randomized algorithm that, for an $m\times n$ matrix whose columns have Euclidean norm at most one, finds a signing with discrepancy below $99$ in expected $\widetilde O(L_{\mathrm{in}}+n^ω)$ bit operations, where $L_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the input encoding length and $ω$ is the exponent of matrix multiplication. The previous fastest algorithm with a constant discrepancy bound, due to Li, is deterministic and uses $O(mn+n^{ω+2}\log^3 n)$ arithmetic operations. We build on the spectral signing framework of Guo, Fang, and Lu and of Li, which rounds a single fractional coloring while one spectral potential controls every row. Li's potential tracks a top eigenvalue, and the gap below that eigenvalue, which can be of order $1/n$, limits the length of every step. We replace it with a resolvent potential that is smooth without any gap condition, and we draw step signs at random, so that the potential only needs to be concave while progress is measured separately. Our key insight is to reuse a single subspace of directions throughout a batch of steps, thereby using only one spectral computation, so that the more expensive linear algebraic operations are paid for only polylogarithmically often at each scale. Within a batch, we sample directions from a Gaussian completion matrix whose inverse we maintain under rank-one row replacements. Finally, we use a finite-precision analysis to prove stability of the algorithm and attain the bit-complexity bound.

title: Four-Level Quantized Soft Information Aided Hard-Decision Decoder for Product-like Codes
summary: We propose a novel low-complexity soft-aided hard-decision decoding scheme for product-like codes, termed iterative bounded-distance decoding (iBDD) with graded scaled reliability and bit-flipping (GSRF). This scheme operates on four-level quantized soft information. It incorporates a graded scaled reliability rule to assign decoding confidence to the bounded-distance decoding result, and employs a bit-flipping rule based on bit-level and component-code-level reliability. A selective re-decoding rule is designed to further facilitate the error performance while keeping the number of BDD attempts in reasonably low levels. The decoding parameter design of iBDD-GSRF is investigated for product codes and staircase codes, respectively. Simulation results on both codes verify that iBDD-GSRF achieves a gain of more than 0.4 dB over the conventional iBDD, comparable to several existing unquantized soft-aided decoders.

title: TraHist: Fast and Accurate Cardinality Estimation for Trajectory Data (Extended Version)
comment: Extended version of the paper to appear in PACMMOD Vol. 4, No. 6 (SIGMOD 2027)
summary: Cardinality estimation is fundamental for query optimization in database systems. Histogram-based estimators are widely used for their simplicity and efficiency but rely on point-centric partitioning that assumes record independence. This assumption breaks in trajectory data, where records from the same moving object show strong spatiotemporal dependencies. Conventional axis-aligned histograms therefore fragment trajectories across partition boundaries, leading to overestimation through duplicate counting. This error reflects a structural limitation of partition boundaries that are misaligned with trajectory-induced density patterns. To this end, we propose TraHist, a histogram-based estimator approximating density-aligned partitioning via efficient grid-based propagation. TraHist builds density-adaptive rectilinear buckets to preserve trajectory continuity and local density coherence while keeping histogram efficiency. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets show that TraHist reduces estimation error by over 20x relative to the strongest competing estimator in query regimes where trajectory fragmentation is a dominant source of estimation error, while maintaining sub-millisecond query latency and competitive construction cost.

title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
summary: Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system requirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output-level reranking or parameter-generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade-offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alternative by reusing multiple objective-specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender systems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross-objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two-stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parameter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learnable preference-to-coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade-off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional generative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and effective controllability while delivers 165--228x faster inference-time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/35798642/RECSOUP.git.

title: Smoothed analysis of policy iteration and value iteration for deterministic discounted and mean-payoff games played on any graph
summary:
Our understanding of turn-based stochastic games is reminiscent of our understanding of linear programming in the 1970s. Instead of the simplex method, we have two families of algorithms - policy iteration and value iteration - which work well in practice but are known to run in exponential time on some input instances, and we still lack an algorithm that runs in polynomial time on all instances.
  A recent result by Loff and Skomra showed that, for deterministic discounted and mean-payoff games played on an ergodic graph, a variant of policy iteration runs in smoothed polynomial time. This offered an explanation of why policy iteration performs well in practice, analogous to Spielman and Teng's explanation for the simplex method.
  In this paper, we drop the ergodicity assumption: we show that their policy iteration algorithms run in smoothed polynomial time for any game graph. We do this by defining a condition number that naturally generalizes theirs, showing that sufficiently-perturbed games are well-conditioned with high probability, and showing that their algorithms are efficient on well-conditioned instances. Although the outline is similar, our proof requires a substantially new approach, based on log-Lipschitz distributions which recently appeared in work on the smoothed analysis of the simplex method.
  For our second contribution, we propose three new value iteration algorithms for solving deterministic mean-payoff games (also on any graph). All three are based on iterative methods for finding fixed points of non-expansive operators, which we show can be applied to the Shapley operator. The first two are simple applications of Krasnoselskii-Mann iteration and Halpern iteration. The third is quadratically faster but more complicated: it runs Zwick-Paterson and Halpern iterations in parallel. We prove that all three algorithms are correct and run in smoothed polynomial time.

title: A 0.4584-approximation for DR-submodular maximization over down-closed convex sets
summary: We obtain a $0.4584$-approximation for nonnegative, non-monotone, $L$-smooth DR-submodular maximization over compact convex down-closed subsets of the unit cube, improving the $4/9\approx0.4444$ ratio of Aggarwal's projection-based algorithm~\cite{aggarwal2026geometry}. A recovery map combining exponential and linear-fractional branches admits a cube-wide affine upper bound. The resulting continuous-time Frank--Wolfe-type algorithm with randomized output and its randomized discrete-time implementation both satisfy $\E F(\widehat x)\ge(0.4584-\varepsilon)\OPT-δLD^2$; the implementation uses polynomially many cube-wide value/full-gradient queries and ordinary linear maximization calls, where $D$ is the feasible diameter and $\varepsilon,δ>0$ are accuracy parameters. Our guarantee and Aggarwal's hardness bound~\cite{aggarwal2026geometry} place the optimal approximation ratio for cube-wide value/full-gradient queries and linear maximization, with additive error $δLD^2$, in $[0.4584,0.4705)$. Standard multilinear sampling and pipage rounding imply an expected $(0.4584-\varepsilon)$-approximation for nonnegative submodular set-function maximization under a matroid constraint \cite[Lemma B.3]{vondrak2013symmetry}.

title: On the Subadditivity of Mutual f-Information
summary: We address an open problem raised by Polyanskiy and Wu in their textbook concerning the subadditivity of mutual \(f\)-information. We study two notions of generalized mutual information: mutual \(f\)-information, defined by \(\widetilde{I}_f(X;Y)=D_f(p_{XY}\|p_Xp_Y)\), and variational \((G,f)\)-information, obtained by minimizing an average of transformed \(f\)-divergences. For the first notion, we derive a sufficient condition on \(g(x)=x^2f''(x)\) that guarantees subadditivity under conditionally independent observations. This condition yields explicit families beyond the previously known examples generated by \(x\log x\) and \((x-1)\log x\). Our proof relies on the concavity of a generalized variance functional. For the variational notion, we extend existing sufficient conditions beyond the transforms \(G(x)\in\{x,\log(1+x),-\log(1-x)\}\). Using a comparison inequality for \(G^{-1}(G(A)+G(B))\), we obtain differential criteria for concave and convex transforms. Explicit constructions illustrate the resulting classes of subadditive information measures.

title: VoteGEO-Bench: Measuring the Impact of Generative Engine Optimization on Electoral Visibility
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for election information, yet little is known about how external web content shapes the political information they present. Generative engine optimization (GEO) rewrites web content to improve its visibility in generated responses. To investigate its potential risks in voting scenarios (VoteGEO), we introduce VoteGEO-Bench, a benchmark covering the 2024 U.S. presidential election and the 2026 Japanese House of Representatives election, combining election-related queries, historical webpages, and voter personas. We first analyze sources cited by generative engines and find that many citations come from lower-cost owned and open-platform sources, while some webpages remain visible across days. We then evaluate 11 rewriting strategies in 4 categories, examining target specification, effectiveness across engines and elections, and the role of voter personas. Rewriting without specifying a target rarely increases target exposure, whereas target-specified rewriting more often does. Strategies that improve page organization or strengthen a position through argumentation yield greater gains than adding supporting evidence or changing wording. For the two strongest strategies, gains remain broadly positive across evaluated U.S. personas, but persona conditioning shows no consistent effect on these gains. Explicit partisan identities can create baseline exposure gaps larger than the gain from rewriting one webpage. When partisanship is implicit in the voter profile, baseline shifts depend on how strongly the engine responds to that signal.

title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions
summary: We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self-interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. In reality, exact clones drive agent profit to zero, violating the natural risk-reward incentives of participants. Conversely, we empirically demonstrate that the opposite extreme, absence of competition, also leads to market failure and value extraction collapse. Between these two extremes, we investigate how heterogeneous agents can survive in markets that span the critical middle ground of imperfect competition. To be profitable, agents learn to strategically shade bids to secure positive individual profit margins, while still ensuring that the marketplace functions effectively enough so that collaborative tasks posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that imperfect competition successfully sustains necessary agent profit margins while maintaining high task success rates at low costs.

title: A General Framework for Matching with Delays
summary: We present a simple deterministic $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for the online minimum-cost perfect matching with delays (MPMD) problem on arbitrary, unknown metric spaces, where $n$ is the (unknown) number of requests. This improves upon the recent $O(\log^5 n)$-competitive algorithm of Dufay and Wattenhofer (SODA 2026) and nearly matches the $Ω(\log n / \log \log n)$ randomized lower bound of Ashlagi et al. (APPROX 2017). Our algorithmic framework rests on two ingredients: an online moat-growing process that grows active dual variables at a deliberately slowed constant rate $α< 1$ to control temporal asymmetry, and a delayed eligibility rule that matches requests in the same dual component only after their waiting time is proportional to their time-expanded distance. The framework extends naturally to arbitrary concave delay functions, maintaining an $O(\log n)$ competitive ratio, and to $k$-way matching with delays, yielding an $O(k \log n)$-competitive deterministic algorithm.

title: Iterative Bounded Distance Decoding With 2-Bit Reliability Marker For Product-Like Codes
comment: Accepted by IEEE Information Theory Workshop 2026
summary: We propose a novel soft-aided hard-decision decoding scheme for product codes based on two-bit quantized reliability markers. In particular, one bit is used for a two-level tolerance miscorrection check to validate the bounded distance decoding (BDD) result, while the other identifies bits to be randomly flipped upon BDD failure and miscorrection. List decoding is incorporated to further facilitate the error performance. Density evolution is performed for the design of the quantization thresholds. Compared to iterative BDD, the proposed scheme requires only moderate increases in memory and computational overhead. Simulation results verify that our scheme outperforms several unquantized soft-aided decoders, while maintaining small memory costs and low BDD attempts.

title: Aligning LLMs with Sparse Retrieval via Adaptive Sparse Supervision
summary: While large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic representations, their application to first-stage retrieval incurs substantial latency and storage costs. Neural sparse retrievers such as SPLADE provide efficient retrieval but rely on relatively compact encoders with limited representational capacity. To bridge this gap, we propose an LLM-based sparse retrieval framework with input-adaptive sparse alignment. Specifically, we introduce a dynamic $α$-truncation strategy that selects input-specific supervision supports based on the cumulative activation mass of SPLADE representations. This strategy guides the LLM to preserve salient lexical signals while suppressing less informative activations, without relying on a fixed support budget. Subsequent retrieval fine-tuning combines contrastive learning, knowledge distillation, and sparsity regularization to improve retrieval effectiveness. Experiments on MS MARCO and six selected BEIR datasets demonstrate improvements over SPLADE++ while maintaining competitive effectiveness against LLM-based sparse retrievers. Compared with Lion-sp, our method reduces index storage by 6.4-fold and end-to-end query latency by over 11-fold, achieving a favorable effectiveness-efficiency trade-off.

title: Testing Connectedness and Edge Connectedness
summary: We revisit the classical problem of testing connectedness of graphs represented in the adjacency lists model and obtain optimal bounds. Specifically, we show that $\varepsilon$-testing connectedness of graphs with maximum degree at most $d$ requires $Ω(\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon d})$ queries (when $\varepsilon \le \frac{1}{4d^5}$). Our result implies that the connectedness tester of Levi, Pallavoor, Raskhodnikova, and Varma ({\em ACM Trans.\ Comput.\ Theory, 2022}) is optimal. We also study the problem of testing $k$-edge-connectedness of both directed and undirected graphs of average degree $\overline{d}$ in the adjacency lists model and design a tester with query complexity $O(\frac{k}{\varepsilon} \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon \overline{d}})$, improving upon the bounds by Forster, Nanongkai, Saranurak, Yang, and Yingchareonthawornchai (SODA 2020). Furthermore, we complement our upper bound by showing that every one-sided error $k$-edge-connectedness tester must make $Ω(k/\varepsilon)$ queries.

title: On the structure of polynomial ideal codes and additive Reed--Solomon codes
summary: We study structural properties of polynomial ideal (PI) codes and additive Reed--Solomon (aRS) codes in the folded Hamming metric (equivalently, the Hamming metric over a larger alphabet). We first determine the maximum possible length of PI codes, prove that the dual of every PI code is a generalized PI code, and deduce that PI codes are dually QMDS together with an explicit formula for their weight distribution. We then show that PI codes defined by irreducible polynomials correspond to aRS codes with pairwise nonconjugate evaluation points. For these aRS codes, the previous results on PI codes apply (duality, QMDS property and weight distribution). We show that, asymptotically, aRS codes with nonconjugate evaluation points achieve the same length as PI codes. We also compute the permutation group of such aRS codes. We also extend the family of PI codes to consider arbitrary polynomial modules (not necessarily pairwise coprime), and study when these and general aRS codes satisfy the QMDS and dually QMDS properties.

title: GACC-Bench: Benchmarking Goal-Adaptive Context Compression Ability across Large Language Models
summary: Context compression in long-running applications of large language models (LLMs) must preserve goal-relevant information, often before specific downstream questions are known. We introduce GACC-Bench, a benchmark for Goal-Adaptive Context Compression that evaluates how reliably LLMs adapt information retention to specified high-level goals. For each source context, we derive one or more high-level goals by grouping source-grounded questions according to shared downstream objectives. The benchmark contains 500 goals and 2,571 questions over 281 document and agent-trace contexts from seven collections spanning diverse domains, with all instances reviewed by human experts. The compressor receives a source context, a goal, and a context-length budget, with the associated evaluation questions withheld. A fixed reader answers these questions individually using the same compressed context. Our evaluation of ten LLM compressors reveals substantial gaps to full-context performance even for the best-performing model, particularly in supporting correct answers to every question associated with a goal. Compared with goal-agnostic compression, target-goal conditioning consistently improves accuracy, whereas mismatched-goal conditioning reduces it. GACC-Bench is available at https://github.com/weiting24/GACC-Bench.

title: Geometric Hashing in MPC with Applications to Clustering and Stochastic Embeddings
summary: In this paper we study consistent hashing (a.k.a. sparse partitions) for doubling metrics in the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. A $(Γ,Λ)$-hash with diameter bound $Δ$ partitions a metric space into clusters of diameter at most $Δ$ such that every ball of radius $Δ/Γ$ intersects at most $Λ$ clusters in expectation. Consistent hashing has emerged as a central tool in geometric MPC algorithms. However, so far it has been solely used in Euclidean spaces, where it can be pre-computed. On the other hand, in cases where the metric space is received as input and unknown in advance, no previous parallel construction was known. We present the first fully scalable MPC algorithm over machines with local space $n^σ$, that given an $n$-point metric space with doubling dimension $d\leq O(σ\log n)$, samples a randomized $(Γ,2^{O(d/Γ)})$-hash in $O(d/σ^3)$ rounds. There is a dichotomy: if the doubling dimension is $d=Ω(σ\cdot\log n)$, a polynomial number of rounds is required to compute such a hash. We conclude by showing that this MPC primitive yields $O(d/σ^3)$-round fully scalable MPC algorithms for a broad class of fundamental geometric problems in doubling metrics, including stochastic tree embeddings with $O(\log n)$ expected distortion, constant factor approximation for facility location, bicriteria $(O(ε^{-2}),1+ε)$-approximation for $k$-median and $k$-means.

title: It Takes Two Moments: Rigidity and Limits of Continuous Encoders for Over-the-Air Computation
summary: We study over-the-air computation of functions, such as empirical variance, formed by combining two separately postprocessed sums of locally transformed observations. We consider continuous encoders subject to pointwise peak-power constraints over a single use of a complex multiple-access channel. With four or more transmitters, we identify conditions under which exact noiseless recovery forces every continuous encoder collection into a common affine structure that preserves both sums, reducing infinite-dimensional encoder design to selecting a finite set of coefficients. To quantify resilience against channel noise, we introduce a robustness score that measures the separation of noiseless received aggregates relative to variations in the desired function value. Within this characterized encoder family, we formulate robustness maximization as an exact convex semi-infinite program, eliminating rank constraints without a relaxation gap, and construct a decoder that attains the minimum uniform noise-amplification constant. For several function classes, including empirical variance, we derive closed-form robustness-optimal encoders and scores. Under mild regularity conditions, we also establish sharp limits on the Gaussian mean squared error at high signal-to-noise ratios and show how using the input distribution reduces average error at the expense of uniform robustness.

title: Decoding Failure Biases IBLT Count Measurements: A Gaussian-Selection Law at the Peeling Threshold
summary:
In a self-sizing set-reconciliation protocol, a small first-round Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT) sketch attempts peeling decoding; after failure, the protocol estimates the difference count $d$ from the count energy and sizes the second round from a lower quantile of the measurement. This quantile must be computed conditionally on failure: the measurement and peeling success are determined by the same random mapping, so conditioning can shift the measurement law.
  In the ideal peeling model, inside the critical window where failure has nondegenerate probability, the standardized energy and a statistic of the unsigned mapping that governs the peeling outcome (the precritical score) have a joint Gaussian limit with correlation $η_kρ^2$, $ρ$ being the sign imbalance and $η_k$ a closed-form constant. The measurement conditional on failure is thus a bivariate normal truncated to a half-plane, which we call the Gaussian-selection law. Since $η_k$ changes sign between $k=4$ and $k=5$, under one-sided imbalance the unconditional threshold undercovers exactly when $k\ge5$ and is conservative for $k=3,4$.
  The key tool is a quenched CLT for a signed quadratic form on a random overlap graph; under asymptotically balanced signs, conditioning on any unsigned mapping event that is permutation-invariant and has probability bounded away from zero leaves the standard normal limit unchanged. After failure the protocol observes the total sign; inverting the selection law yields an upper confidence bound for $d$, asymptotically conservative in the critical window and, when $d/\sqrt M\to\infty$, along the whole load axis. The experiments use analytic constants, none fitted; the unconditional threshold carries a selection error that does not vanish with scale, while the corrected selection-law threshold matches per-configuration empirical quantiles.

title: How Does Probabilistic Constellation Shaping Control Ranging Sidelobe Levels in ISAC?
summary: Probabilistic constellation shaping (PCS), originally designed to fill the gap between finite uniform constellations and continuous capacity-achieving input distributions, has recently emerged as a central tool in adjusting the expected integrated sidelobe level (EISL) in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). In this paper, we show that PCS goes beyond EISL: A large class of PCS methods, termed as type-based PCS, are capable of providing precise control over codeword-wise integrated sidelobe level ratio (ISLR) for systems employing orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), thus yielding a stronger sensing performance guarantee than EISL control. We further show that OFDM is almost the only unitary modulation basis whose codeword-wise ISLR can be precisely controlled by type-based PCS. Based upon the analytical results, practical type-based PCS methods compatible with the probabilistic amplitude shaping (PAS) framework are conceived, which achieve higher communication rates than existing ISAC-oriented PCS methods under identical ISLR constraints.

title: Incremental Exact Vertex Connectivity
summary:
We study the problem of maintaining the vertex connectivity $κ$ of a graph under edge insertions. For undirected graphs, our algorithm uses $O(κ^4 \log^2 n)$ amortized time per edge insertion. After each edge insertion, the algorithm outputs the current value of $κ$, plus a set of $κ$ vertices whose removal disconnects the graph. Our algorithm is Monte-Carlo randomized and works with a randomness-adaptive adversary. The algorithm also works on directed graphs against an oblivious adversary, which is equivalent to an output-adaptive adversary if we only have to output the current value of $κ$.
  Previously, algorithms for maintaining the vertex connectivity with $o(n)$ time per edge insertion were only known for $κ\le 2$, and need $\tilde{O}(\log^2 n)$ and $O(\sqrt{n})$ time per edge insertion for $κ= 1,2$, respectively. Moreover, for $κ> 4$, no algorithm faster than recomputation from scratch was known.
  We complement our algorithm with a conditional lower bound: Under the OMv conjecture, any insertions-only algorithm that outputs the current value of $κ$ after every insertion needs $Ω(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ amortized time per edge insertion for $κ= Θ(n)$. Previous conditional lower bounds for this problem only apply to worst case running time, or algorithms that support both edge insertions and edge deletions.

title: Fisher Information and Support Complexity of Gaussian Mixtures
summary:
We study lower bounds on the Fisher information of Gaussian location mixtures and their applications to estimation problems. First, for a discrete mixing distribution, we derive a universal positive-semidefinite lower bound on the Fisher information matrix in terms of the Rényi entropy of order two. For a mixing distribution supported on $K$ points, this bound scales as $\log(K)/K^2$, improving by a logarithmic factor on the support-size dependence obtained from Stam's inequality. We then develop dimension-aware trace bounds using classical Sobolev inequalities. These bounds are expressed in terms of Sibson's $α$-mutual information and yield the scaling $K^{-2/n}$ in dimension $n$. A complementary bound involving the $α$-mutual information of order $1/2$ is obtained using the sharp Young convolution inequality.
  The derived inequalities are further specialized to rotationally invariant mixing distributions supported on discrete spherical shells. In this setting, an intrinsic-dimensional bound on Sibson mutual information leads to lower bounds on the Fisher information in terms of the number of occupied shells. As applications, we study least favorable priors for bounded Gaussian mean estimation. In the scalar case, we show that the least favorable prior on $[-R,R]$ has at least $Ω(R\sqrt{\log R})$ support points and that each of its probability masses is of order at most $1/R$. In the vector case, we show that the number of occupied shells grows at least linearly with $R$. Finally, Brown's identity and the I-MMSE relationship are used to translate the Fisher-information inequalities into upper bounds on the MMSE and mutual information.

title: Preprocessed 3SUM: From Reals to Integers
summary:
The Preprocessed 3SUM problem asks to preprocess a set $A$ of $n$ numbers so that we can quickly decide whether a query subset $A' \subseteq A$ contains a solution $a+b=c$. The best known query bounds differ substantially between integer and real inputs. For integers, a series of advances with near-quadratic preprocessing reduced the query time from $\tilde O(n^{13/7})$ [Chan, Lewenstein; STOC '15] to $\tilde O(n^{11/6})$ [Chan, Vassilevska W., Xu; STOC '23], and finally to $\tilde O(n^{3/2})$ [Kasliwal, Polak, Sharma; SOSA '25]. For reals, only the first of these bounds has been achieved, by adapting the corresponding integer algorithm [Fischer; SODA '25]. Is this gap inherent to the more limited tools available for real inputs?
  We give a randomized real-to-integer reduction with $\tilde O(n^2)$ preprocessing overhead and no asymptotic increase in query time. This yields $\tilde O(n^2)$ preprocessing and $\tilde O(n^{3/2})$ query time for real inputs, closing the gap. We show how to extend our result to the setting where one set is unknown at preprocessing time. Our reduction is conceptually simple, and relies on an interesting technical toolkit around old and new tools from sparse linear algebra. More broadly, it suggests a route to real-to-integer reductions for other additive problems.

title: Short-Boundary Signaling for Asynchronous Grant-Free Control-to-Control Communications
summary: In asynchronous grant-free access, receivers must detect variable-length transmissions and identify their start and end. Existing decoder-aided receivers use start and tail sequences which are as long as one codeword, causing substantial overhead for short commands. This paper treats the boundary (i.e., start and tail sequences) length as an independent design parameter and proposes a convolutional neural network that detects both boundaries from the received waveform and the decoder soft output. Its waveform input size decreases with the boundary length, while the decoder input keeps the codeword length, so the boundary can be shortened without altering the decoder. Analysis and simulations quantify the resulting tradeoff among payload efficiency, collision exposure, and boundary detection. The results show that the proposed receiver can exploit very short boundaries: in the considered setting, the shortest tested boundary, $L_{\mathrm{b}}=16$, yields the highest effective payload efficiency at all tested loads, whereas a correlation-based benchmark with the same sequences performs best with $L_{\mathrm{b}}=64$ at moderate and high loads.

title: Parameterized Complexity of Isometric Path Cover: Treewidth and Diameter
summary:
We study the fixed-parameter tractability of the \textsc{Isometric Path Cover} problem where, given an integer $k$ and a simple, undirected, and unweighted graph $G$, the objective is to decide whether $G$ admits a set of $k$ isometric paths (i.e., shortest paths between their endpoints) whose union is the entire vertex set of $G$.
  We show that \textsc{Isometric Path Cover} is NP-hard on graphs of pathwidth (and thus treewidth) at most 287. This is an interesting contrast with the closely related problems \textsc{Isometric Path Partition} and \textsc{Path Cover}, which are both known to be XP for treewidth, see [Chakraborty et al., WG 2026] and [Foucaud et al., TCS 2026].
  On the positive side, we show, by a suitable dynamic programming scheme, that \textsc{Isometric Path Cover} admits an XP algorithm w.r.t.~the parameter combination of treewidth and diameter, running in time $n^{\diam^{O(\tw)}}$ where $\diam$, $\tw$, and $n$ denote the diameter, the treewidth, and the number of vertices of the input graph, respectively.
  However, we also prove that \textsc{Isometric Path Cover} becomes W[1]-hard for pathwidth on graphs of diameter~7, showing that an XP algorithm is the best one can hope for w.r.t.~this parameterization, under standard complexity theory assumptions.

title: Model-Driven Deep Learning for Distributed Detection with Low-Bit Quantization
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures. Accepted by IEEE JSAC
summary: Distributed detection plays a fundamental role in communication-efficient collaborative inference over large-scale networks, where spatially distributed nodes must cooperate using severely quantized messages due to bandwidth constraints. While low-bit quantization is essential for reducing communication overhead, it can significantly degrade detection performance, particularly when prior knowledge of observation noise is unavailable. To address this challenge, we propose a model-driven deep learning framework for distributed detection with low-bit quantization. For fixed local quantizers, we first derive the exact finite-sensor maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection error and prove that, under conditionally independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations, independent local randomizations, and a common quantization-level constraint, identical quantizers preserve the supremum of the average network Chernoff information. Guided by these results, we develop a binary probabilistic quantizer with a trainable neural probability controller and design a tree-structured probabilistic quantizer for scalable multi-bit quantization. The exact finite-sensor MAP error provides the training objective for the binary quantizer, while we derive a computationally tractable Bhattacharyya surrogate objective for training the multi-bit quantizer. For both cases, we derive analytical MAP fusion rules based on the class-conditional probability mass functions (PMFs) of the quantized messages. When the observation statistics are unknown, these PMFs are estimated from held-out labeled data, yielding plug-in MAP detectors. Simulation results show that the proposed method approaches centralized-oracle performance at higher quantization resolutions and remains effective under changes in network size and test-time signal amplitude.

title: Asteroidal Triples and Friends in (Likely Necessary) Matrix Multiplication Time
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures; to appear at SODA 2027
summary:
In a seminal paper, Kratsch and Spinrad [SODA 2003 and SIAM Journal on Computing 2006] studied several important problems in structural graph theory that anticipated two trends in fine-grained complexity, both from the upper- and lower-bound side:
  * From the upper-bound side, for each of these problems the authors give an intermediate running time strictly between $n^ω$ and $n^3$, where $ω<2.371177$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. When optimized, this running time can be made $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+ω)/2})$. By now, many more problems can be solved in this running time: directed unweighted or node-weighted APSP, a variety of matrix products such as max-min and dominance, RNA Folding and many more. For some of these, the community has also developed tools suggesting that this intermediate running time is necessary.
  * From the lower-bound side, the authors give lower bounds of $n^{ω-o(1)}$, conditioned on three natural hardness hypotheses on the complexity of quantified variants of triangle detection that account for different types of hardness of such problems.
  Despite this, it has remained open for over 20 years which of these two pieces of evidence reflects the truth for the problems that Kratsch and Spinrad study: whether the intermediate running time is indeed necessary and stronger lower bounds hold, or whether the hardness evidence of Kratsch and Spinrad is essentially tight. In this paper, we resolve this question and show that the latter is the case: all problems admit an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^ω)$ time algorithm.
  As an additional contribution, we make partial algorithmic progress on further problems in structural graph theory of intermediate complexity, improving over previous work [Chiu and Lu, STACS 2022 and Information and Computation 2024][Spinrad, Discrete Applied Math 2004].

title: Legitimate Reconstruction Advantage in Wiretapped Semantics-Aware Remote Monitoring
summary: This paper investigates joint accuracy and security in semantics-aware remote monitoring, where source updates intended for a legitimate receiver may also be intercepted by an eavesdropper. We define legitimate reconstruction advantage (LRA) as the joint event that the intended receiver correctly reconstructs the current source state using received updates while the eavesdropper reconstructs it incorrectly. Source evolution changes the relevance of received updates at the two receivers, so their marginal reconstruction accuracies do not, in general, determine the probability of this joint event. Under randomized stationary (RS) transmission and zero-order-hold reconstruction at both receivers, we derive an explicit joint stationary distribution and closed-form expressions for LRA probability and persistence for general finite-state ergodic Markov sources. For two-state and uniform-transition sources, we obtain algebraic expressions that enable low-complexity optimization of RS policies. Analytical and numerical results show that maximizing the probability of legitimate advantage need not maximize its persistence. For two-state sources, rare-transmission analysis reveals that, at a fixed sum of transition probabilities, greater transition asymmetry can increase persistence while reducing LRA probability. Moreover, optimizing marginal accuracy and security metrics can select policies that are suboptimal for LRA. Counterintuitively, more frequent transmission or improved legitimate-channel reliability can increase legitimate reconstruction accuracy while reducing LRA probability. Finally, a geofencing application translates prescribed LRA requirements into spatial constraints on eavesdropper locations.

title: Per-State Signatures and Mean Time-to-Failure: An Algorithm for Systems With Simultaneous Failures
comment: The manuscript has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Reliability
summary: We present an algorithm that computes the structural signature and the mean time-to-failure (MTTF) of a monotone binary system at every one of its states, rather than only at the state in which all components work. It makes no assumption on the structure function and evaluates it exactly once per state, as many times as needed for the signature of the complete system alone, so computing the MTTF everywhere costs only a factor polynomial in the number of components over computing it once. As a by-product, it identifies all minimal path sets. We assume exchangeable component failure times whose survivor count is a continuous-time Markov chain. This setting admits simultaneous failures, as in the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin, binomial failure rate and lethal-shock models, where the simplifications available for single failures do not apply. We use the per-state MTTF to define threshold repair policies. We show that the per-state signature is a strictly finer decision criterion than the MTTF: signature dominance at a common failure count implies MTTF dominance, but not conversely. Under the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin model the MTTF is monotone in the state, which yields the long-run cost rate of every threshold policy in a single pass. Experiments on 22 benchmark networks with up to 30 components and 31 failure models show that the best MTTF-threshold policy has a median excess cost of 0.36% over the optimal state-based policy, and that it is never worse than the best policy that repairs after a fixed number of failures.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Federated Learning for Joint Communication and Computation in XR Systems
comment: 18 pages, 16 figures, 3 tables. This paper has been accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing
summary: The convergence of communication and computation, empowered by artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced capabilities, emerges as a key enabler for realizing the promising functionalities of the sixth-generation of communication systems (6G). To this end, this paper investigates an AI-native, robust network, where multiple base stations (BSs) simultaneously serve several extended reality (XR) devices. The paper then presents an innovative distributed deep learning-based approach to simultaneously manage the transmit and computing powers, and computation allocation, amidst uncertainties in both channel and computing states information. Under such an interference network scenario, the paper proposes a robust approach for minimizing the worst-case delay across the served XR devices, subject to computation and power constraints. The paper leverages a deep neural network (DNN) that can be trained either centrally or in a federated manner to map estimated channels and computation requirements to optimized resource allocations per BS. During training, uncertainty samples, reflecting both channel and computing estimation errors, are injected after the DNN output to account for such joint uncertainties. Our results validate the enhanced robust delay performance and scalability of joint uncertainty injection as compared to uncertainty-agnostic methods and state-of-the-art benchmarks, with federated learning-based solutions achieving near-centralized performance while enhancing efficiency, privacy, and adaptability.

title: Tree Edit Distance: Near-Linear-Time Approximate, Sublinear, and Dynamic
summary:
Tree edit distance (TED), the analog of string edit distance (ED) for hierarchical data, is the minimum number of node insertions, deletions, and substitutions transforming one labeled rooted ordered tree into another. We narrow polynomial gaps between TED and ED in near-linear-time approximation, sublinear algorithms, and dynamic algorithms.
  We give an $n^{o(1)}$-approximation in $O(n)$ time and, for every $0<δ<1$, a $(\log n)^{O(1/δ)}$-approximation in $O(n^{1+δ})$ time. This improves the previous near-linear-time $O(\sqrt n)$-approximation [Boroujeni et al., STOC'19] and brings TED to parity with ED in this regime up to polylogarithmic factors.
  With query access to the balanced-parentheses (Euler-tour) representation of the input trees, we give the first sublinear-time TED algorithm: for every $τ\in[1,n]$, it computes a $τn^{o(1)}$-approximation of $1+\mathrm{ted}$ in $O(n/τ)$ time.
  For dynamic TED, we give an exact algorithm with amortized update time $\tilde{O}(k^7)$ and a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation with amortized update time $\tilde{O}_{\varepsilon}(k)$, where $k$ caps the distance that must be reported. The exact algorithm is the first to beat recomputation in a nontrivial parameter regime. The approximation improves prior dynamic guarantees [Das et al., FOCS'25] and cannot be significantly improved in any parameter regime without a breakthrough for static $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation of ED.
  All results use dynamic programming on a new hierarchical tree decomposition, analogous to partitioning strings into blocks of geometrically decreasing sizes. It combines structural properties previously achieved only in isolation, providing a framework for transferring algorithmic ideas from ED to TED, with additional ingredients addressing the obstacles in each computational setting.

title: Design of a Family of Rate-Adaptive LDPC Convolutional Codes with Short Constraint Length
summary: This paper studies the design of some high-rate, adaptive, low-density parity-check (LDPC) convolutional codes with short constraint length, based on interleaved parity-check polynomials. Starting from some known results regarding the selection of polynomials that yield codes free of short cycles in the associated Tanner graphs, we propose some new constructions based on Golomb rulers, along with relaxed variants that do not strictly satisfy the Golomb ruler condition, but retain similar structural properties. The result is a family of rate-adaptive code constructions with code rates of the form $R=(n_0-1)/n_0$. Conditions for the absence of length-4 cycles are derived, together with upper bounds on the free distance that are met in all considered examples.

title: Subgraph Counting with Local Node Differential Privacy
comment: To appear at the ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA) 2027
summary:
We study the problem of approximately counting subgraphs under local node differential privacy (LNDP), a recently introduced model that enforces strong privacy guarantees in analyses of distributed social networks. We design a noninteractive $(\varepsilon,0)$-LNDP algorithm that, given any public $k$-node template graph $H$, counts occurrences of $H$ in a sensitive undirected $n$-node graph with additive error $O(n^{k-\frac{1}{2}}/\varepsilon^{k-1})$, for any constant $k$. We complement this algorithm with a lower bound showing that every noninteractive $(\varepsilon,δ)$-LNDP algorithm for counting copies of any $k$-node template graph with maximum degree greater than $1$ must have error $Ω(n^{k - \frac{1}{2}})$. Thus, our algorithm achieves optimal error for counting constant-size subgraphs, up to $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors.
  Our results substantially expand the types of network statistics known to be approximable under LNDP: prior work considered only functions of the degree distribution. In addition, our lower bound yields the first known $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ gap between central and local node differential privacy when accuracy is required for all input graphs. Previous separations either only involved $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors or only applied to promise problems.

title: Minimizing Age of Incorrect Information in Pull-Based Remote Estimation of a Markov Source
summary: In this paper, we consider a discrete-time pull-based remote estimation system involving an information source and a remote monitor where the information source is a finite-state irreducible discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) process. In this system, the remote monitor sends a pull request towards the source which responds by sampling its process so as to transmit the sampled values towards the monitor through a delay channel, encapsulated in information packets. We consider i) zero delay (ZD) and ii) unit delay (UD) channels, where the packet transmission times are zero and one slot, respectively. For remote estimation, we use the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator, and for quantifying its performance, we use the mean age of incorrect information (MAoII) which is a recently proposed freshness and mismatch metric that penalizes an incorrect estimation along with its duration. Our goal is to obtain pull policies so as to minimize MAoII under a long-run sampling rate constraint. For the ZD model, we propose a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) formulation of the problem, which allows us to find the optimum observation-dependent pull policy. On the other hand, the UD channel prevents the monitor from possessing perfect information on the actual AoII process at any given time, and the SMDP formulation of the ZD channel cannot readily be used for the UD model. For the system with the UD channel, we first provide a numerical algorithm to calculate the MAoII and the average sampling rate for a given observation-dependent pull policy. For the optimization of the underlying remote estimation system, we use the joint distribution of the age and source processes to be obtained from the history of all observations, termed as belief. Subsequently, we propose a belief-dependent policy obtained via the belief-MDP formulation and a constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) algorithm.

title: Near-Optimal Parallel $M$-Matrix Scaling
summary: In this paper we consider the problem of computing a positive diagonal scaling of a $d \times d$ symmetric $M$-matrix so that all row and column sums are $1$. We provide a poly-logarithmic iteration algorithm that solves this problem to high accuracy, where the cost of each iteration is dominated by the cost of solving a Laplacian system. This improves upon the recent $\tilde{O}(d^{1/3})$ iteration bound of [Vladu STOC 2025] and yields a randomized algorithm for the problem that runs in near-linear time and poly-logarithmic parallel depth.

title: The Information Bottleneck is NP-hard
summary: Given a joint distribution $P_{XY}$ on a finite alphabet, the information bottleneck method seeks a representation $T$ of $X$ that is as informative as possible about $Y$ while compressing $X$, where $T$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given $X$. We show that computing the optimal value $\mathrm{IB}(P_{XY},R) = \sup_T \{ I(Y;T) : I(X;T) \le R \}$ of the information bottleneck problem, as well as its Lagrangian relaxation $L_β(P_{XY}) = \sup_T \big[I(Y;T) - βI(X;T)\big]$, is NP-hard. Moreover, unless $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}$, neither $\mathrm{IB}(P_{XY},R)$ nor $L_β(P_{XY})$ can be approximated in polynomial time within an additive error of order $|\mathcal{X}|^{-3/2}$.

title: When Fresh Information Is Not Enough: Age-of-Actuation-Optimal Scheduling for Energy-Harvesting Actuators
summary: We study transmission scheduling in an energy-harvesting actuation system where an actuation requires both a received update and available energy. While age of information (AoI) measures information freshness, age of actuation (AoA) measures the time elapsed since the latest completed actuation. The transmitter observes the receiver's AoA and battery state and decides whether to transmit a fresh update in each slot. We formulate average-AoA minimization as a Markov decision process and establish an AoA-threshold property for an optimal policy. We also derive the average AoA in closed form under the AoI-optimal policy, which is always-transmit. Numerical results show that AoA-aware scheduling can improve actuation freshness while reducing the number of transmissions, although information freshness may deteriorate. The two policies coincide for some pairs of channel success and energy-arrival probabilities. For a one-unit battery, the transmission rate under the AoA-optimal policy can vary nonmonotonically with the energy-arrival probability.

title: Decoding Failure Biases IBLT Count Measurements: A Gaussian-Selection Law at the Peeling Threshold
summary:
In a self-sizing set-reconciliation protocol, a small first-round Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT) sketch attempts peeling decoding; after failure, the protocol estimates the difference count $d$ from the count energy and sizes the second round from a lower quantile of the measurement. This quantile must be computed conditionally on failure: the measurement and peeling success are determined by the same random mapping, so conditioning can shift the measurement law.
  In the ideal peeling model, inside the critical window where failure has nondegenerate probability, the standardized energy and a statistic of the unsigned mapping that governs the peeling outcome (the precritical score) have a joint Gaussian limit with correlation $η_kρ^2$, $ρ$ being the sign imbalance and $η_k$ a closed-form constant. The measurement conditional on failure is thus a bivariate normal truncated to a half-plane, which we call the Gaussian-selection law. Since $η_k$ changes sign between $k=4$ and $k=5$, under one-sided imbalance the unconditional threshold undercovers exactly when $k\ge5$ and is conservative for $k=3,4$.
  The key tool is a quenched CLT for a signed quadratic form on a random overlap graph; under asymptotically balanced signs, conditioning on any unsigned mapping event that is permutation-invariant and has probability bounded away from zero leaves the standard normal limit unchanged. After failure the protocol observes the total sign; inverting the selection law yields an upper confidence bound for $d$, asymptotically conservative in the critical window and, when $d/\sqrt M\to\infty$, along the whole load axis. The experiments use analytic constants, none fitted; the unconditional threshold carries a selection error that does not vanish with scale, while the corrected selection-law threshold matches per-configuration empirical quantiles.
